questions.key_step: Write $a:b:c=7:6:5$ from the three sums and apply the cosine rule three times.
questions.justification: Routine: one parametrisation, then three cosine-rule evaluations; no insight needed, proof format.

questions.key_step: $AD=BD$ gives $B=\frac A2$ (or $\cos\frac A2=\frac a2$), which with the sine/cosine rule gives $A=60^\circ$.
questions.justification: Bisector length plus cosine rule, two equations in one unknown; routine multi-step chain.

questions.key_step: Reduce to $\frac1{\sin B}+\frac1{\sin C}=\frac1{\sin A}$ for angles $\frac\pi7,\frac{2\pi}7,\frac{4\pi}7$ by sum-to-product and $\sin\frac{4\pi}7=\sin\frac{3\pi}7$.
questions.justification: Unfamiliar heptagon identity, a numerical answer with no options and an exact trig identity at the end; idea availability is moderate.

questions.key_step: $\frac bc=\frac{\sin3C}{\sin C}=4\cos^2C-1$ and $\sin\frac A2=\cos2C$.
questions.justification: Sine rule plus triple-angle identity, two short deductions; routine chain with a proof format.

questions.key_step: Median formula plus the right angle at $B$ gives $4b^2=7c^2$; then $\cos\angle ABD=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
questions.justification: Median formula, Pythagoras in the small triangle and one cosine rule; routine chain, answer 120 degrees.

questions.key_step: Locate the orthocentre at $OD=2r$ on the axis and set $AO+OD=AD$ with $AO=2R\cos A$.
questions.justification: Needs the orthocentre-on-incircle observation, three standard formulas and a careful half-angle simplification with no options to check against.

questions.key_step: Express $AE$ from $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle AEC$ with the sine rule and equate, giving $\cos2\alpha=\frac12$.
questions.justification: Two sine-rule applications with an equation in one angle; routine but needs the figure set-up.

questions.key_step: Recognise $A=90^\circ$ from $\frac a{2R}=1$, then compute the two bisectors as hypotenuses of right triangles.
questions.justification: Right-triangle recognition followed by exact surd computation with no options; precision risk but each step is standard.

questions.key_step: Relate the two circumradii to the diagonals, $BD:AC=R_1:R_2$, then use the right-angled diagonal triangle.
questions.justification: Two circumradius relations and a half-angle step; numerical answer with several linked stages.

questions.key_step: Recognise $\frac{\cot C}{\cot A+\cot B}=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2c^2}$.
questions.justification: One standard identity applied once, then substitution; same family as the 2021 cot-ratio question but with less computation.

questions.key_step: Supplementary opposite angles turn the area into $ab\sin120^\circ$ and the common diagonal gives $a^2+b^2$.
questions.justification: Two equations in two unknowns from area and the cosine rule; routine chain, no insight needed.

questions.key_step: The centre moves on a circle of radius $\frac{7R}8$; the cosine rule in the triangle of centres gives $120^\circ$ and the arc spans $120^\circ$.
questions.justification: Needs a clear model of the moving circle and its extreme positions, then a cosine rule and arc length; a numerical answer with an easy-to-misread configuration.

questions.key_step: Convert $\cos(A-B)$ to $\tan\frac{A-B}2$ and apply Napier's analogy to get $C=90^\circ$.
questions.justification: A short chain using a less common formula (Napier's analogy) but only two steps; numerical answer.

questions.key_step: All three conditions are equivalent to $A=B$; (iii) needs $xy+yz+zx=1$.
questions.justification: A three-way proof where the third condition needs the half-angle tangent identity and a factorisation; statements need genuine checks.

questions.key_step: Cosine rule gives $a^2-4\sqrt3a+10=0$ with two positive roots: two triangles.
questions.justification: Standard ambiguous-case question; one quadratic and an area step.

questions.key_step: Write the four areas in $\theta=\frac\pi n$; then $A_2^2=A_1B_1$ and the half-angle identity gives the H.M. relation.
questions.justification: Standard formulas and two short trig verifications; a proof with routine chain.

questions.key_step: Use $r_a=R(1+\sin B+\cos B)$ for a right angle at $A$ (rather than the inradius formula).
questions.justification: Exradius of a right triangle, half-angle simplification and two angle values to choose from; several linked stages with a risk of using the wrong circle.

questions.key_step: Get $\tan\frac A2=\frac{r-\rho}{2\sqrt{r\rho}}$ for each vertex circle, then use $\sum\tan\frac A2\tan\frac B2=1$.
questions.justification: Non-routine geometric modelling (common tangent of touching circles gives half-angle tangents), then a long exact algebraic step with no options.

questions.key_step: Recognise $S$ as the incircle ($r=1$, $h_a=3$) so that $PB\cdot PC=(s-b)(s-c)$ is fixed.
questions.justification: Idea of identifying the circle as an incircle (or using the symmetric picture) then a short computation; moderate idea availability.

questions.key_step: Convert $AH,BH,CH$ to $2R\cos$ and use $\sum\cos^2=1-2\prod\cos$ to get a cubic in $R$.
questions.justification: Three parts with a hidden identity and a cubic; several stages but each is a standard formula.

questions.key_step: Heron plus the Ravi substitution reduces the claim to $(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)\ge8xyz$.
questions.justification: Needs the substitution idea (or Euler) but each step is standard; a proof with an equality case to state.

questions.key_step: Write $I_n$ and $O_n$ in $\theta=\frac\pi n$ and use $\frac{I_n}{O_n}=\cos^2\theta$.
questions.justification: Two area formulas and a double-angle identity; routine proof, the only subtlety is the sign of the square root.

questions.key_step: $\frac xc=\sin B$ etc., so the sum is $\sum a\sin A$.
questions.justification: One recognition step and the sine rule; paragraph-based single correct with options.

questions.key_step: Express both sums through $a^2+b^2+c^2$ using $x=\frac{bc}{2R}$ and $\cot A=\frac{2R\cos A}a$.
questions.justification: Two standard sums and a ratio; longer algebra than Q23 but no insight beyond standard identities.

questions.key_step: Recognise $c\sin B=b\sin C=x$ so each fraction is $2$.
questions.justification: One recognition step; no computation. Easiest of the paragraph set.

questions.key_step: Parametrise the A.P. and use the exterior angle theorem and the right triangle $ABD$ to find the angles.
questions.justification: Angle chasing with an A.P. parametrisation; several linked steps before the circumcircle, paragraph with options.

questions.key_step: Right angle at $B$ puts $O$ at the midpoint of $AC$, so $\triangle BOC$ is equilateral.
questions.justification: Once the triangle is known (from Q26) this is two standard facts; routine.

questions.key_step: $BB'=2\times$ the altitude from $B$ to $AC$.
questions.justification: One standard formula after the triangle is known; routine.

questions.key_step: Four independent one-idea items: $\lambda=2+2\cos A$, $\sum\tan=\prod\tan$, $R\cos A=r$, Napier's analogy.
questions.justification: Four items, two need an identity to recall and one a short Napier computation; no item is deep but all four must be right.

questions.key_step: Right angle at $A$ gives $r_1r_2=r(r+r_1+r_2)$; (B) needs the monotonicity argument, (D) the contact-point lengths.
questions.justification: Four geometric items, one of which has a flawed key; item (B) needs a careful monotonicity argument and (D) a non-routine tangent-length idea.

questions.key_step: Napier's analogy gives $C=90^\circ$; the four items then follow from the right triangle.
questions.justification: One unlocking step (right angle at C) after which each item is routine; same data as Q13.
